entry.sum: To count a collection is to pair its objects one-to-one with the number words one, two, ..., $n$; the last word $n$ is the number of objects, and an empty collection has number 0. The answer does not depend on the order of counting, the next word always names one more, and from $a$ to $b$ there are $b - a + 1$ numbers. The English number names follow rules (with exceptions below twenty) that the numerals record, and counting in equal steps of $m$ reaches $m \times k$ after $k$ steps.
key: |A| = n \iff A \text{ pairs one-to-one with } \{1, \dots, n\}
entry.why: Every later idea about whole numbers, from comparison and addition to place value and multiplication, rests on counting and on the fact that the next number is one more; the pairing definition is also where combinatorics, the pigeonhole principle and the theory of infinite sizes begin.

links.note: Counting a set by pairing it one-to-one with a set already counted is the basic method of enumerative combinatorics; the pigeonhole principle is the fact that a one-to-one map from [m] into [n] exists only when m <= n.
The off-by-one (fencepost) error, confusing b - a with b - a + 1, is one of the commonest bugs in programs that loop over ranges.

blocks.body: Counting answers the question how many: you say the number words in their fixed order, pairing each word with one object, and the last word said is the number of objects. Two facts make this work and both need a reason: the answer does not depend on the order in which the objects are counted, and adding one object moves the count on to the next word. Together they make the whole numbers $0, 1, 2, 3, \dots$ the sizes of finite collections, which is where comparison, arithmetic and place value begin.

blocks.title: Counting a collection
blocks.body:
The number words one, two, three, ... form a list that is always said in the same order. The start of the list is learnt by heart, and later words are built by rules (see the third section). Counting a collection means pairing its objects with the first words of that list.

Anything that can be told apart can be counted: objects, sounds, steps, the letters of a word. What must be fixed first is what counts as one object: the word BANANA has 6 letters but only 3 different letters, and both answers are correct counts of different things.

blocks.title: Counting, and the number of a collection
blocks.body:
To count a collection, say the number words in order starting from one, and attach each word to one object, so that every object gets exactly one word and no object gets two. Stop when every object has a word. The last word said is the number of objects in the collection. A collection with no objects has number zero, written 0.

In the language of sets (see [[sets-relations]]), write $$[n] = \{1, 2, \dots, n\}$$ for the first $n$ counting numbers, with $[0]$ the empty set. More generally, a map from a set $A$ into a set $B$ is one-to-one when different elements of $A$ go to different elements of $B$. A pairing of two sets in which every element of each set has exactly one partner in the other is a one-to-one correspondence, or bijection. A set $A$ has $n$ elements, written $|A| = n$, when $A$ can be paired one-to-one with $[n]$. A correct count of $A$ that ends at the word for $n$ is exactly such a pairing: the object that gets the word for $k$ is the partner of $k$.

blocks.title: Pairing lemma
blocks.body: If there is a one-to-one map from $[m]$ into $[n]$, then $m \le n$. Hence if $[m]$ and $[n]$ can be paired one-to-one, then $m = n$.

By [[induction]] on $m$. If $m = 0$, then $m \le n$ for every $n$.

Now suppose the claim holds for $m$, and let $f$ be a one-to-one map from $[m + 1]$ into $[n]$. Since $m + 1$ goes somewhere, $n \ge 1$. Make $m + 1$ go to $n$: if it goes to some $j \ne n$ and some $i \le m$ goes to $n$, swap, sending $m + 1$ to $n$ and $i$ to $j$; if nothing goes to $n$, just send $m + 1$ to $n$. Either way the map is still one-to-one. Now remove $m + 1$ and $n$: no element of $[m]$ goes to $n$, so what is left is a one-to-one map from $[m]$ into $[n - 1]$. By the induction hypothesis $m \le n - 1$, that is, $m + 1 \le n$.

A pairing of $[m]$ with $[n]$ is a one-to-one map each way, so $m \le n$ and $n \le m$, and $m = n$.

blocks.title: The count does not depend on the order
blocks.body:
If a collection is counted correctly twice, in any two orders, the two counts end at the same word. In symbols: if $A$ can be paired one-to-one both with $[m]$ and with $[n]$, then $m = n$.

In particular, moving the objects, from a line into a circle or a heap, does not change their number, because it does not change which objects there are.
Follow the first pairing from $[m]$ to $A$ and then the second back from $A$ to $[n]$. This pairs $[m]$ one-to-one with $[n]$, so $m = n$ by the pairing lemma.

blocks.title: The last word gives the number only from one
blocks.body: A count of $n$ objects that starts at the word $s$ ends at the word $n + s - 1$, so the last word is the number of objects only when $s = 1$: counting five objects from three ends at seven, and the number is $7 - 3 + 1 = 5$, not 7.

items.q: How many letters does MISSISSIPPI have, and how many different letters? Say what is being paired with the number words in each count.
items.hint: In the second count, each letter shape is one object, however often it appears.
items.solution: 11 letters: the eleven letter positions are paired with one to eleven. 4 different letters: M, I, S and P are paired with one to four.

items.q: Twelve dots in 3 rows of 4 are counted row by row and then column by column, as in the figure. The dot in row $r$ and column $c$ gets the word $4(r - 1) + c$ in the first count. Which word does it get in the second? Which dots get the same word in both counts?
items.hint: Column by column, the first $c - 1$ columns hold 3 dots each.
items.solution: In the second count it gets $3(c - 1) + r$. The words agree when $4r - 4 + c = 3c - 3 + r$, that is, $3r - 2c = 1$. With $r$ from 1 to 3 and $c$ from 1 to 4 the only solutions are $r = 1, c = 1$ and $r = 3, c = 4$: the first dot gets 1 and the last gets 12 in both counts, and every other dot changes its word. The positions depend on the order; the last word does not.

items.q: Prove that if $A$ and $B$ can be paired one-to-one and $|A| = n$, then $|B| = n$.
items.hint: Join the pairing of $[n]$ with $A$ to the pairing of $A$ with $B$.
items.solution: Let each $k$ in $[n]$ go to its partner in $A$, and that element to its partner in $B$. Each $k$ reaches exactly one element of $B$, and each element of $B$ is reached from exactly one $k$ (go back the same way). So $B$ is paired one-to-one with $[n]$ and $|B| = n$. This is how combinatorics counts a set: by pairing it with a set already counted.

items.q: Five letters are put into four envelopes. Use the pairing lemma to show that some envelope gets at least two letters.
items.hint: If no envelope got two letters, what kind of map would letter to envelope be?
items.solution: Number the letters 1 to 5 and the envelopes 1 to 4. If no envelope got two letters, sending each letter to its envelope would send different letters to different envelopes: a one-to-one map from $[5]$ into $[4]$. The pairing lemma would then give $5 \le 4$, which is false. So some envelope gets at least two letters (the [[pigeonhole]] principle).

blocks.title: One more, counting on and counting back
blocks.body: Each word in the list has a next word. The fact that links the order of the words to the sizes of collections is that the next word names one more. It is what lets you count on from a number you already know instead of starting again from one.

blocks.title: The next number is one more
blocks.body: If $|A| = n$ and $x$ is an object not in $A$, then $A$ with $x$ added has $n + 1$ elements, where $n + 1$ is the number named by the word after $n$. If $n \ge 1$, removing one object from $A$ leaves $n - 1$ elements.

Count $A$, ending at the word for $n$, and then give $x$ the next word. Every object of the larger collection now has exactly one word, so this is a correct count, and it ends at the next word. By the order theorem, every other correct count ends there too. For removal, count $A$ so that the object $y$ to be removed comes last. This is a re-ordering of a correct count (swap the words of $y$ and of the last object), so it is again a correct count, and by the order theorem it ends at $n$. The count of the remaining objects is the same count, stopped one word earlier.
A list has 8 entries and 3 more are added. How many entries are there, without counting the 8 again?
blocks.solution: The 8 are already counted, so count on: give the new entries the words after eight, namely nine, ten, eleven. By the theorem, used three times, the list has 11 entries. Counting on 3 from 8 is the first form of the sum $8 + 3 = 11$ (see [[addition-subtraction]]). Counting back works the same way in reverse: taking 3 away from 11 is ten, nine, eight. Counting back stops at zero, because 0 has no number before it among the whole numbers.

blocks.title: How many numbers from a to b
blocks.body: For whole numbers $a \le b$, the list $a, a + 1, \dots, b$ contains $b - a + 1$ numbers, and going from $a$ to $b$ in steps of one takes $b - a$ steps.

Pair each number $x$ of the list with $x - a + 1$, which is a counting number because $x \ge a$. Then $a$ goes to 1, each next number to the next counting number, and $b$ to $b - a + 1$; going back, $k$ comes from $k + a - 1$. So the list is paired one-to-one with $[b - a + 1]$ and has $b - a + 1$ numbers. For the steps: each step of one lands on a number after $a$, different steps land on different numbers, and each of $a + 1, \dots, b$ is landed on by one step. So the steps are paired with the list without $a$, and there are $b - a + 1 - 1 = b - a$ of them.

fig = plt.gcf(); fig.set_size_inches(6.4, 2.3)
ax = fig.add_axes([0, 0, 1, 1])
ax.plot([14.5, 25.5], [0, 0], color='black', lw=1.2)
t = np.linspace(0, np.pi, 40)
for n in range(15, 26):
    ax.plot([n, n], [-0.08, 0.08], color='black', lw=1.0)
    said = 17 <= n <= 23
    ax.plot(n, 0, 'o', ms=8, mfc='blue' if said else 'white', mec='blue' if said else 'black', zorder=3)
    ax.text(n, -0.32, str(n), ha='center', va='center', fontsize=11)
for a in range(17, 23):
    ax.plot(a + 0.5 - 0.5 * np.cos(t), 0.14 + 0.45 * np.sin(t), color='orange', lw=1.6)
ax.text(20, 0.85, '6 steps of one: 23 - 17 = 6', ha='center', fontsize=11)
ax.plot([17, 17, 23, 23], [-0.55, -0.65, -0.65, -0.55], color='blue', lw=1.2)
ax.text(20, -0.9, '7 numbers said (blue): 23 - 17 + 1 = 7', ha='center', fontsize=11)
ax.set_xlim(14.3, 25.7); ax.set_ylim(-1.1, 1.1); ax.axis('off')
blocks.caption: Counting on from 17 to 23 says 7 numbers (blue dots) but takes 6 steps of one (orange arcs): $23 - 17 = 6$ steps and $23 - 17 + 1 = 7$ numbers. On a [[number-line]] the numbers are points and the steps are the gaps between neighbouring points.
blocks.alt: A number line from 15 to 25. The dots at 17, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22 and 23 are filled blue; the others are open. Six orange arcs join each blue dot to the next, labelled 6 steps of one: 23 - 17 = 6. A blue bracket under 17 to 23 is labelled 7 numbers said (blue): 23 - 17 + 1 = 7.

blocks.title: Steps or numbers: the fencepost error
blocks.body: Subtracting $23 - 17 = 6$ counts the steps between the numbers, not the numbers themselves, which are one more. The same slip is called the fencepost error: a straight fence 30 feet long with posts every 3 feet has $30 / 3 = 10$ sections but 11 posts. Before subtracting, decide whether you are counting the gaps or the points, and whether both ends are included.

blocks.title: Amount and position
blocks.body: The same words do two jobs. In a count from one, the $k$-th object gets the word $k$, so the last object's position is the amount. In a count from $s$, the $k$-th object gets $k + s - 1$, every word is $s - 1$ ahead of the position, and the last word overstates the amount by $s - 1$.

items.label: Amount
items.body: Five as the size of a collection (cardinal): it answers how many, and by the order theorem it is the same whichever count is made.

items.label: Position
items.body: Fifth as the place of one object in a particular count (ordinal). Position depends on the order: in another count a different object is fifth.

blocks.body: Count on from 96 to 104. How many numbers are said, and how many after 96?
blocks.solution: Ninety-six, ninety-seven, ninety-eight, ninety-nine; after ninety-nine the next word is one hundred; then one hundred and one, one hundred and two, one hundred and three, one hundred and four. The list has $104 - 96 + 1 = 9$ numbers, and $104 - 96 = 8$ of them come after 96: counting on 8 from 96 reaches 104.

items.q: How many whole numbers $n$ satisfy $17 < n \le 40$?
items.hint: Write the list with both ends included first.
items.solution: The list is $18, 19, \dots, 40$, since 17 itself is excluded. It has $40 - 18 + 1 = 23$ numbers. (Taking $40 - 17 = 23$ also works here, because it counts the steps from 17, which land exactly on $18, \dots, 40$.)

items.q: A chapter runs from page 37 to page 52, both included. How many pages is it?
Counting back from 20 you say 20, 19, 18, ... and stop after 7 words. Where do you stop?
Twelve trees stand in a straight row, equally spaced, and the first and last are 55 metres apart. How far apart are neighbouring trees?
items.hint: Count the gaps, not the trees.
items.solution: Twelve trees have $12 - 1 = 11$ gaps, so each gap is $55 / 11 = 5$ metres.

items.q: Explain why counting on 3 from 8 gives the same result as counting all 11 objects from one.
items.hint: Use the order theorem to choose the order of the full count.
items.solution: Count all the objects so that the 8 old ones come first. That count reaches eight at the last old object, and the new ones then get nine, ten, eleven: exactly the words said when counting on. By the order theorem, every correct count of the 11 objects ends at the same word as this one.

blocks.title: Number names and numerals
blocks.body: Numerals are written with the ten digits 0, 1, 2, ..., 9. From ten on a numeral has two or more digits, and why the position of a digit carries its meaning is the subject of [[place-value]]. The spoken English names follow rules of their own, with exceptions near the start, and it pays to see exactly what they are.

blocks.title: English number names to 999
blocks.body:
1. Zero to twelve have their own words: zero, one, two, ..., ten, eleven, twelve.
2. Thirteen to nineteen end in -teen, which means plus ten, and say the ones first: fourteen is four and ten. Thirteen and fifteen alter the ones word.
3. The whole tens are twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, sixty, seventy, eighty, ninety; -ty means tens. Forty has no u, although four does.
4. From 21 to 99, a number not ending in 0 is named tens first, with a hyphen: twenty-one, forty-six, ninety-nine.
5. From 100 to 999 the name is the hundreds word followed, unless the last two digits are both 0, by the name of the last two digits: three hundred and forty-two (on the and, see below).
Read seventy-three, fourteen and six hundred and fourteen as arithmetic, and write their numerals.
blocks.solution: Seventy-three is 7 tens and 3: $7 \times 10 + 3 = 73$. Fourteen is $4 + 10 = 14$: the name says the 4 first, the numeral writes the 1 first. Six hundred and fourteen is $6 \times 100 + 14 = 614$; its name says six, four, ten while its numeral writes 6, 1, 4. In general, eleven and twelve are own words wherever they occur (four hundred and eleven), and every other name from thirteen up shows its hundreds, tens and ones, in the numeral's order except when the last two digits are 13 to 19, which put the ones first. Eleven and twelve show no parts because they are very old: they probably once meant one left and two left, that is, left over after counting ten, and the parts wore away long ago.

blocks.title: Thirteen or thirty, 17 or 71
blocks.body: Thirteen and thirty sound alike, but -teen means plus ten ($13 = 3 + 10$) and -ty means tens ($30 = 3 \times 10$). And although seventeen says the seven first, the numeral puts the tens digit first: seventeen is 17, seventy-one is 71.

rows.text: British English puts and after hundred: one hundred and twenty-five. American schools often teach one hundred twenty-five, without and, although many Americans say and.
The National Curriculum in England speaks of counting in multiples of 2, 5 and 10; the Common Core calls this skip-counting.

items.solution: forty; fourteen; four hundred and eighteen; four hundred and eighty.

items.q: How many of the names of the numbers 1 to 99 are written with a hyphen?
items.hint: Count the numbers that do not get a hyphen.
items.solution: No hyphen for 1 to 9 (9 names), 10 to 19 (10 names) and the whole tens 20, 30, ..., 90 (8 names): 27 in all. So $99 - 27 = 72$ names have a hyphen, namely the numbers from 21 to 99 not ending in 0.

items.q: How many times is the digit 7 written when all the numerals from 1 to 100 are written down? Why is 77 counted twice?
items.hint: Count sevens in the ones place and in the tens place separately.
items.solution: In the ones place: 7, 17, 27, ..., 97, that is 10 times. In the tens place: 70, 71, ..., 79, that is 10 times. Total 20. The number 77 has a 7 in both places, so it appears in both lists; we are counting digits written, not numbers.

items.q: Explain why any ten consecutive whole numbers contain exactly one multiple of ten, and why their ones digits are $0, 1, \dots, 9$, each once.
items.hint: Write the first number as $10q + r$ with ones digit $r$, and see what happens to $10q + r + i$ as $i$ goes from 0 to 9.
items.solution: Let the numbers be $a, a + 1, \dots, a + 9$ and write $a = 10q + r$ with $0 \le r \le 9$. For $i \le 9 - r$, $a + i = 10q + (r + i)$ has ones digit $r + i$, which runs through $r, \dots, 9$. For $i \ge 10 - r$, $a + i = 10(q + 1) + (r + i - 10)$ has ones digit $r + i - 10$, which runs through $0, \dots, r - 1$. So each digit 0 to 9 appears exactly once in the ones place. A number is a multiple of ten exactly when its ones digit is 0, so exactly one of the ten is a multiple of ten.

blocks.title: Counting in steps
blocks.body: Counting in twos says every second word of the count: 2, 4, 6, 8, ...; counting in fives says 5, 10, 15, 20, ...; counting in tens says 10, 20, 30, .... It is quicker when objects come in equal groups, such as pairs, rows of a table or coins of one value, and it gives the same answer as counting in ones.

blocks.title: Counting equal groups in steps
blocks.body: For whole numbers $m$ and $k$, write $m \times k$ for the number of objects in $k$ groups of $m$ objects, that is, the word at which a count in ones of all of them ends. Counting in steps of $m$ from 0 means that each step moves $m$ words on in the list of number words. If a collection consists of $k$ groups of $m$ objects, counting it in steps of $m$, one step per group, ends at $m \times k$, the same number as counting it in ones. So the $k$-th number of the count in steps of $m$ from 0 is $m \times k$.

Count in ones, group by group, which the order theorem allows. We show by [[induction]] on $j$ that after $j$ groups the count in ones and the count in steps stand at the same word. After 0 groups both stand at 0. If they agree after $j$ groups, then the next step moves the count in steps $m$ words on, while the count in ones gives the $m$ objects of the next group the next $m$ words, so by the one-more theorem, used $m$ times, it also moves $m$ words on. So they agree after $j + 1$ groups. After $k$ groups the count in ones has counted every object, so it stands at $m \times k$ by definition, and so does the count in steps (see [[multiplication]]).

Below the numbers, four dashed orange arcs each jump 5, from 0 to 5, 5 to 10, 10 to 15 and 15 to 20, labelled fives (dashed): 4 jumps, 5, 10, 15, 20.

blocks.body: Count in tens from 23 to 63, and say why the ones stay the same. How many numbers are said?
blocks.solution: 23, 33, 43, 53, 63. The ones stay the same because of the rule that ten more keeps the ones digit: a number with $t$ tens and ones digit $u$ is $10t + u$ (see [[place-value]]), and $10t + u + 10 = 10(t + 1) + u$, which has the same ones digit $u$ and one more ten. So each step of ten keeps the 3 and moves the tens digit on: 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. There are $(63 - 23)/10 = 4$ steps of ten, and one more number than steps, so $4 + 1 = 5$ numbers are said, as in the previous section.

items.q: Someone counts in fives: 5, 10, 15, 20, 30. What went wrong, and how many fives have really been counted at 30?
items.solution: 25 is missing: from 20 to 30 is two steps of five. Since $30 = 5 \times 6$, the word thirty stands for 6 groups of five, not the 5 groups that were stepped.

items.q: A list is made by counting in steps of 4 from 12 to 60. Someone says it has $60 - 12 + 1 = 49$ numbers. What is wrong, and how many numbers does it have?
items.hint: Which step size does $b - a + 1$ assume?
items.solution: The formula $b - a + 1$ counts the numbers in steps of one. In steps of 4 there are $(60 - 12)/4 = 12$ steps, and one more number than steps: 13 numbers, namely $12, 16, \dots, 60$. In general a count from $a$ to $b$ in steps of $m$ says $(b - a)/m + 1$ numbers when $m$ divides $b - a$.

items.q: How many multiples of 3 lie between 100 and 200?
items.hint: Find the first and the last one, then count steps of 3.
items.solution: The first is $102 = 3 \times 34$ and the last is $198 = 3 \times 66$. From 102 to 198 there are $(198 - 102)/3 = 32$ steps of 3, so $32 + 1 = 33$ multiples. Equivalently, they are $3 \times k$ for $k = 34, \dots, 66$, and $66 - 34 + 1 = 33$.

items.q: Counting in threes from 0, is 99 said? Is 100?
items.solution: 99 is said, as the 33rd number, since $3 \times 33 = 99$. The next number is $3 \times 34 = 102$, so 100 is skipped: it is not of the form $3 \times k$.

items.q: Explain why counting in twos from 1 never says an even number, while counting in twos from 0 says every even number.
items.hint: Write the $k$-th number of each count.
items.solution: From 0 the numbers are $2 \times k$ for $k = 0, 1, 2, \dots$, and every even number has this form, so each is reached. From 1 the numbers are $2k + 1$, each one more than an even number, and no number is both even and odd (see [[odd-even-numbers]]).

blocks.title: Looking ahead
blocks.body:
Pairing leads to the [[pigeonhole]] principle and to infinite sets. The pairing lemma says that a one-to-one map from $[m]$ into $[n]$ needs $m \le n$, so putting more than $n$ objects into $n$ boxes puts two in one box. For infinite sets this fails: the even numbers $0, 2, 4, \dots$ pair one-to-one with all the whole numbers, $2k$ with $k$, although they are only part of them. Comparing infinite sizes by pairing is the subject of [[ordinals-cardinals]].

One more leads to [[induction]]. The next word is the successor operation, from which the whole numbers can be built from axioms, and an argument that passes from $n$ to $n + 1$, like the proof of the pairing lemma, is a proof by induction.

Counting in steps leads to [[multiplication]]. Counting $k$ groups in steps of $m$ is the first meaning of $m \times k$, and rules such as $3 \times 4 = 4 \times 3$ are proved by counting one collection in two ways, as the grid of 12 dots was counted by rows and by columns.

- Counting pairs the objects with the words one, two, ..., $n$; the last word $n$ is the number, and it does not depend on the order, because a one-to-one map from $[m]$ into $[n]$ forces $m \le n$.
- The next number is one more; from $a$ to $b$ there are $b - a + 1$ numbers and $b - a$ steps.
- English names: own words to twelve, -teen (ones first) to nineteen, then tens before ones, as in the numeral.
- Counting $k$ groups of $m$ in steps of $m$ ends at $m \times k$, as counting in ones does.
